translations.text: Memoirs written by Ambrose, a leading man of Greece, who became a Christian. All his fellow senators denounced him, and he fled from them.
He wrote and showed them all their folly. At the beginning of his discourse he spoke as follows:
Do not suppose, men of Greece, that I separated myself from your customs without deliberation or good reason. For I explored the whole of their learning:
poetry, rhetoric, and philosophy. When I found nothing sound or worthy of the divine nature, I wished to explore the wisdom of the Christians as well,
and to learn and see who they were, and when it arose, and what was new and foreign about it, or what good things those who
profess this wisdom relied upon. To tell the truth, men of Greece, when I examined it, I found none of the foolishness found in the celebrated Homer,
who spoke about the wars of two nations: because of Helen, he says, many Greeks perished at Troy, far from their beloved home.
For first they say of Agamemnon, their king, that because of the madness of his brother Menelaus, his violent lust, and his uncontrollable desire,
he wished to come and rescue Helen from a certain barbarian shepherd. But when the Greeks won the war and burned the cities and took the women and children captive,
and the land was filled with blood and the rivers were filled with corpses, Agamemnon himself was found captive to desire for Briseis. And Patroclus, they say, was killed,
and Achilles, the son of the goddess Thetis, mourned for him, they say. Hector, they say, was dragged along, and Priam and Hecuba wept over the loss of their children.
And Astyanax, Hector’s son, they say, was thrown from the walls of Ilium, while Ajax the Great carried off his mother Andromache.
And the man who took her captive died a little later through lust. But who can recount the schemes and killings of Odysseus, the son of Laertes?
For in a single day his house became a tomb for a hundred and twenty suitors and was filled with corpses and blood. And he
who gained praise through his wickedness, because he was devoid of excellent wisdom—he whom they say floated on the sea
and heard the voice of the Sirens because he stopped his ears with wax. As for Achilles himself, the son of Peleus,
who leaped across the river, ran to Troy, and killed Hector—this very champion of yours became Polyxena’s slave.
He was overcome by an Amazon as she lay dead. He took off his armor and put on mourning clothes, and in the end he was sacrificed for love. So much for the heroes.
You would have deserved forgiveness, Homer, if your empty discourse had gone only so far as to tell tales about human beings, and not about the gods.
For I am ashamed even to repeat the things said about the gods. These fabricated stories are very wicked and offensive,
and they are refuted and not believed; when pressed, they become ridiculous. For anyone who examines them will laugh, and will not believe them when he hears them.
For these gods, not one of whom kept the laws of justice, chastity, and self-restraint, instead lived as adulterers and in debauchery, yet were not condemned to death as they deserved.
For the lord of the gods, that father of gods and human beings, as you call him, was not merely an adulterer.
That would have been a small thing: he also killed his father and lusted after boys. First, then, I will speak of his adultery, though I am ashamed.
For he appeared to Antiope as a satyr, flowed over Danaë as gold, became a bull for Europa, and a swan for Leda.
But the love of Semele, the mother of Dionysus, also exposed her own burning passion, as well as the jealousy of chaste Hera. And Ganymede the Phrygian
he seized in the form of an eagle, so that, he said, the handsome and beautiful boy would be his cupbearer. And that lord of the gods killed his father Cronus to take possession of his kingdom.
Oh, how many accusations stand against the lord of the gods! How many death sentences he deserves for adultery [?] and sorcery,
and for loving boys! Read out to the lord of the gods, O Greek men, the law against killing one's father, the condemnation of adultery,
and the shame of the disgraceful love of boys. How many adulterers the lord of the gods has taught! How many lovers of boys, sorcerers, and murderers!
For if someone is found who has lusted, let him not die: he did this to imitate the lord of the gods. And if a murderer is found,
he has an easy way out in the lord of the gods. And if someone is a sorcerer, he learned it from the lord of the gods. And if
he is a lover of boys, the lord of the gods is his advocate. But if someone speaks of bravery,
Achilles was braver than the lord of the gods, for he killed the man who killed his friend. But the lord of the gods wept over his son Sarpedon when he died,
grieving over him. And Pluto, who is a god, abducted Kore. Kore's mother hurried about looking for her daughter in every deserted place.
And Alexander Paris, when he abducted Helen, paid the penalty as a lover who had used force. But Pluto, who is a god and abducted Kore, remained without disgrace.
And Menelaus, who is a human being, knew how to search for his wife Helen. But Demeter, who is a goddess, did not know where to look for her daughter Kore.
Let jealousy leave Hephaestus, and let him not be envious. For he was hated because he was old and lame, while Ares was loved because he was young and handsome in appearance.
Then the adultery was exposed, for Hephaestus had not been aware of the love between his wife Beltis and Ares. But when Hephaestus learned of it, he said:
“Come and see this ridiculous and senseless deed: how Beltis, the child of the lord of the gods, dishonors me, who belong to her—me, who am her own—and honors Ares, who is a stranger to her.”
And the lord of the gods was not displeased, for he loved things like these. But Penelope remained a widow for twenty years,
waiting for her husband Odysseus. She occupied herself with work and practiced her crafts, while all those suitors pressed her.
But Beltis, who is a goddess, abandoned her husband Hephaestus when he approached her, because she was overcome by love for Ares.
Listen, Greek men! Which of you would dare to do this, or could even bear to see it? And if anyone should dare,
what torment awaits him, or what lashes! Yet Cronus, who is a god, ate all those children,
and was not even brought to court. But they say that only his son, the lord of the gods, escaped him, and that the madness of his father Cronus was outwitted,
because Rhea, his wife, the mother of the lord of the gods, handed him a stone in place of her son, the lord of the gods, so that he would not eat him.
Listen, Greek men, and consider this madness. For a dumb animal grazing in the wilderness
knows its food and does not approach unfamiliar food. Wild animals, creeping creatures, and birds also know their food. But about human beings
I need not speak. You yourselves know their food and can distinguish it. But Cronus, who is a god,
Not recognizing his food, he bit a stone. Therefore, Greek men, if you want to have gods like these,
do not blame one another when you do such things. And do not be angry with your son when he plans to kill you,
because he is imitating the lord of the gods. And if someone commits adultery with your wife, why do you consider him an enemy, while the lord god whom he resembles
you worship and serve? And why do you blame your wife when she commits adultery and goes unpunished, while you honor Beltis and set her in temples?
Persuade Solon to repeal his laws, and Lycurgus not to establish laws. Let them dissolve their Areopagus and no longer pass judgment.
Let the Athenians no longer have a council. Let the Athenians acquit Socrates, for he came nowhere near resembling Cronus. And let them not kill Orestes for killing his mother.
For look: the lord of the gods did worse things than these to his father. Oedipus, too, hastily brought harm upon himself
by blinding his eyes because he had unknowingly killed his father. For he did not consider the lord god, who killed his father and remained unpunished.
The Corinthians expel Medea [?], who killed her children, yet they worship and honor Cronus, who ate his children.
And Alexander Paris was right to abduct Helen, imitating the god Pluto, who abducted Kore. Let men be freed from the law,
and let cities belong to wanton women and become a dwelling place for magicians. Therefore, Greek men, since your gods are base like you,
and your heroes are valiant, as your dramas relate and your histories proclaim—but as for the sufferings of Orestes and the bed of Thyestes,
and the defilement of Philip, and [?], who was killed out of jealousy and mutilated by his sons in their drunkenness—even Thyestes’ banquet was demanded by his corpse.
And Procne still cries out as she flies, and her sister, whose tongue was cut out, chirps. And what should be said about the murder committed by Oedipus,
who married his mother, and about his brothers, who were his sons, killing one another? I also hate your festivals.
For there are no poems performed there, and to sweet flutes that dispel anxiety they sing with trembling.

And the preparation of the ointments with which you anoint yourselves, and the wreaths you put on! In your great wickedness you have forgotten shame. Your minds have been blinded, you have been put to the test by lust, and you have loved the bed of deceit.
If these things had been said by someone else, they would perhaps bring an accusation against him that they were untrue.
But your own poets tell them, and your hymns and dramas proclaim them. Come now, be instructed in the word of God and in comforting wisdom.
Rejoice and share in it. Know the king who does not perish, and become acquainted with his servants, who do not boast of weapons
or commit murders. For our commander does not desire a large army, but a pure soul, which he has surrounded with a wall of righteousness.
The word of God teaches us at all times, as do the promises of our good king and the works of God.
O soul purchased by the power of the word! O trumpet of peace without war! O teaching that extinguishes the soul’s fire!
It does not produce poets or train philosophers, nor does it have public orators. Rather, it leads the mortal onward and brings him across, so that we may not die.
And it raises human beings from the earth as gods to the realm above the firmament. Come and become like me, for I too was once like you.
The end.
